tip: Marinating overnight in the fridge transforms these from good to extraordinary — the lemon and olive oil tenderise the chicken significantly and the oregano becomes more fragrant after a long rest.

name: Roasted Red Pepper & Tomato Frittata with Manchego
description: A golden, set frittata billowing with sweet roasted peppers, blistered cherry tomatoes, and melted Manchego — finished under the grill until the top is just set and lightly bronzed. Light enough for a spring lunch, substantial enough for a weeknight supper, and infinitely adaptable. The kind of dish that proves eggs are anything but boring.
kidNote: Slice into wedges like pizza — children invariably love frittata. Swap Manchego for mild cheddar if preferred.
ingredients: 2 roasted red peppers from a jar, sliced
steps: Preheat the grill to high. Beat the eggs in a large bowl, season well with salt and pepper, and set aside.
Heat the olive oil in a 26cm ovenproof frying pan over medium heat. Cook the shallot for 3–4 min until softened, then add the garlic and cook for 1 min.
Add the roasted peppers and cherry tomatoes and cook for 2–3 min until the tomatoes begin to collapse.

Pour the beaten eggs over the vegetables and gently shake the pan to distribute. Cook over medium-low heat for 6–8 min, pulling the edges in with a spatula so uncooked egg flows to the sides, until the base is set but the top is still slightly wobbly.
Scatter over the Manchego and slide the pan under the hot grill for 3–4 min until the top is just set and lightly golden.
Leave to cool in the pan for 5 min before slicing. Scatter with basil leaves and serve with a green salad.
tip: Low-and-slow on the hob before the grill finish is key to a silky rather than rubbery frittata. If the base is setting too fast, reduce the heat — patience here pays off.

name: Turkish Eggs with Whipped Yoghurt & Chilli Butter
description: Silky whipped garlic yoghurt spread into wide bowls, topped with softly poached eggs that break at the touch and flood the yoghurt with golden yolk. A sizzling pour of chilli butter — fragrant with Aleppo pepper and dried mint — streaks across the top, turning a handful of ingredients into something extraordinary. Sourdough toast for dragging through it all is non-negotiable.
kidNote: Reduce the chilli butter to plain melted butter with just a pinch of paprika for children. Younger eaters enjoy the creamy yoghurt base with the egg yolk stirred through.
ingredients: 1 tsp Aleppo pepper flakes or ½ tsp regular chilli flakes
steps: Whisk together the yoghurt, garlic, lemon juice, and a generous pinch of salt until smooth. Divide between four wide, shallow bowls and spread out with the back of a spoon.
Bring a wide pan of water to a gentle simmer. Add the vinegar. Swirl the water, crack in two eggs at a time, and poach for 3 min until the whites are set and the yolks are runny. Keep warm.
While the eggs poach, melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Once foaming, add the Aleppo pepper, dried mint, and paprika. Swirl for 30 seconds until fragrant — watch it doesn't burn.
Place two poached eggs on top of the yoghurt in each bowl.
Spoon the sizzling chilli butter over the eggs, making sure some streaks across the yoghurt.
Garnish with fresh dill and serve immediately with plenty of toasted sourdough.
tip: The yoghurt must be at room temperature before serving — cold yoghurt straight from the fridge will chill the eggs immediately and the dish loses its magic. Take it out 30 min before.

name: Baked Eggs in Spiced Butternut & Tomato Sauce
description: Eggs cracked directly into a bubbling, sweet-savoury sauce of butternut squash and spiced tomatoes — baked until the whites are just set and the yolks quiver. The sauce is lush, deeply coloured, and carries warmth from cumin and harissa. Tear crusty bread through the whole thing and this becomes one of those meals that stops people in their tracks.
kidNote: Reduce the harissa to ½ tsp and the eggs sitting in the sauce are naturally appealing to children. Serve with plenty of bread for scooping.
ingredients: 500g butternut squash, peeled and cut into 2cm cubes
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Heat the olive oil in a large, ovenproof frying pan or skillet over medium heat. Cook the onion for 6 min until softened, then add the garlic, cumin, paprika, and harissa. Cook for 2 min.
Add the butternut squash, chopped tomatoes, and stock. Stir well and simmer for 15 min until the squash is just tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Taste the sauce and season well. Use a spoon to create eight small wells in the sauce.
Crack an egg into each well. Transfer the pan to the oven and bake for 8–10 min until the whites are just set but the yolks are still runny.
Remove from the oven and rest for 2 min — the residual heat continues to cook the eggs, so pull them out slightly before you think they're done.
Scatter with fresh coriander and serve directly from the pan with crusty bread.
tip: Oven temperatures vary considerably — start checking at 8 minutes. You want whites that are opaque but yolks that wobble freely. Once set, the yolk firms fast.

name: Harissa Roasted Cauliflower with Chickpeas & Tahini
description: Cauliflower florets roasted at high heat until the edges blacken and caramelise, tossed in rose harissa alongside golden chickpeas. Draped with a silky, lemony tahini dressing and finished with pomegranate seeds and mint, this is vegetarian food with serious presence — bold, colourful, and anything but an afterthought.
kidNote: Reduce the harissa to a mild version or just ½ tsp for children. Roasted cauliflower with tahini dressing is frequently a surprising hit even without the heat.
steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C/200°C fan. Toss the cauliflower florets with 2 tbsp harissa and 2 tbsp olive oil. Season and spread on a large roasting tray in a single layer.
Toss the chickpeas with the remaining harissa and olive oil on a separate small tray.
Roast for 25–30 min, turning halfway, until the cauliflower is deeply caramelised and charred at the edges and the chickpeas are crisp.
Make the tahini dressing: whisk together the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and enough cold water to make a smooth, pourable sauce. Season with salt.
Spread the tahini dressing across a large serving platter. Pile the roasted cauliflower and chickpeas on top.
Scatter with pomegranate seeds and mint, and serve with flatbreads or rice.
tip: Give the cauliflower room — overcrowding the tray causes steaming rather than roasting. Use two trays if necessary, and rotate them halfway through cooking.

name: Creamy Mushroom, Thyme & Taleggio Risotto
description: Slow-stirred Arborio rice swelling into a rich, ivory risotto perfumed with earthy mushrooms, fresh thyme, and the famous funk of melted Taleggio — a cheese that turns unctuous and runny when it hits the heat, coating every grain. This is patience rewarded: 25 minutes of stirring that results in something deeply, uncommonly good.
kidNote: Taleggio has a strong flavour — swap for mild fontina or a simple grating of cheddar for younger eaters. The risotto itself is mild and creamy.
ingredients: 200g Taleggio, rind removed and torn into pieces
steps: Soak the dried porcini in 200ml of boiling water for 15 min. Strain through a fine sieve, reserving the soaking liquid, and roughly chop the porcini. Add the strained soaking liquid to the hot stock.
Heat 1 tbsp butter and the olive oil in a large, wide saucepan over high heat. Cook the fresh mushrooms and porcini for 5–6 min until golden. Season and set aside.
Add 1 tbsp butter to the same pan over medium heat and cook the onion for 6–7 min until softened. Add the garlic and thyme and cook for 1 min.
Add the rice and stir for 2 min until the grains are coated and toasted. Pour in the wine and stir until fully absorbed.

Add the hot stock a ladleful at a time, stirring continuously and waiting for each addition to be absorbed before adding the next. This process takes 18–22 min — the rice should be creamy and just al dente.
Remove from heat, fold in the cooked mushrooms, Taleggio, remaining butter, and Parmesan. Cover and rest for 2 min before serving.
tip: The porcini soaking liquid is liquid gold — strained and added to the stock, it doubles the mushroom depth in the risotto without any extra effort.

name: Aubergine Parmigiana with Fresh Basil & Mozzarella
description: Layers of golden-fried aubergine interleaved with a rich tomato sauce, torn mozzarella, and fresh basil — baked until bubbling, bronzed on top, and fragrant with olive oil and garlic. This Southern Italian classic is vegetarian comfort food at its most generous: built for sharing, made for lingering over, and even better the following day.
kidNote: Aubergine parmigiana is naturally mild and very appealing to children who like pizza flavours. Cut into smaller portions and serve with garlic bread.
ingredients: 2 x 125g balls mozzarella, drained and torn
crusty bread or green salad, to serve
steps: Preheat the oven to 190°C/170°C fan. Salt the aubergine slices and leave in a colander for 15 min, then pat dry with kitchen paper.

Heat a good slug of olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the aubergine slices in batches for 2–3 min per side until golden brown, adding more oil as needed. Drain on kitchen paper.
Make the tomato sauce: fry the garlic in 1 tbsp olive oil for 1 min, then add the chopped tomatoes and sugar. Season well and simmer for 15 min until thick.

Spread a thin layer of tomato sauce in the base of a 25x20cm baking dish. Layer over a third of the aubergine, then spoon over more sauce, scatter with basil, and add some torn mozzarella and Parmesan. Repeat two more times, finishing with sauce, mozzarella, and Parmesan.
Bake for 25–30 min until the top is deep golden and bubbling.
Rest for 10 min before serving — this helps the layers hold together when cut.
tip: Salting and drying the aubergine removes bitter moisture but also means it absorbs far less oil when frying. The difference in the finished dish — less greasy, more savoury — is significant.

name: Tuscan White Bean & Cavolo Nero Soup with Rosemary Oil
description: A deeply satisfying Italian ribollita-inspired soup — cannellini beans simmered with cavolo nero, tomato, and Parmesan rind until thick and silky, with a fragrant drizzle of rosemary-infused oil to finish. This is peasant cooking elevated by time and patience: unassuming to look at, extraordinary to eat, and better the next day.
kidNote: Blend the soup fully for younger eaters who balk at leafy greens. Serve with plenty of torn bread for dunking — the rosemary oil can be left out for children.
ingredients: 200g cavolo nero or kale, stalks removed and roughly chopped
steps: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrot, and celery for 8–10 min until very soft. Add the garlic and cook for 2 min.
Add the chopped tomatoes, cannellini beans, stock, and Parmesan rind if using. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 min.
Remove about a third of the beans with a ladle, mash roughly, and stir back into the soup — this gives the broth a silky, thickened body.
Add the cavolo nero, push it down into the liquid, and cook for a further 10 min until wilted and tender. Discard the Parmesan rind. Season well.
Meanwhile, gently warm 4 tbsp olive oil in a small pan with the rosemary sprigs and crushed garlic for 5 min — do not let it boil. Strain into a small jug.
Ladle the soup into bowls, drizzle generously with rosemary oil, and serve with crusty bread.
tip: Simmering a Parmesan rind in the soup costs nothing and adds weeks of flavour — the glutamates leach out slowly, giving the broth an umami depth that's difficult to achieve otherwise.

name: Butternut Squash, Sage & Ricotta Stuffed Pasta Shells
description: Jumbo pasta shells packed with a pillowy mixture of roasted butternut squash, ricotta, Parmesan, and nutmeg, baked in a browned-butter sage sauce until the edges of the pasta blister and the filling turns molten and golden. This is cold-weather vegetarian cooking at its most elegant — rich, aromatic, and deeply comforting.
kidNote: Sweet squash and mild ricotta make this a reliable crowd-pleaser for children. Top individual portions with extra grated cheese before baking.
ingredients: 600g butternut squash, peeled and cut into 3cm cubes
50g Parmesan, grated, plus extra to top
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Toss the squash in 2 tbsp olive oil, season, and roast for 25–30 min until very tender and caramelised. Cool slightly, then mash until smooth.
Cook the pasta shells in well-salted boiling water for 2 min less than the packet instructions — they'll finish in the oven. Drain carefully and spread on an oiled tray.
Mix the mashed squash with the ricotta, Parmesan, nutmeg, and plenty of seasoning. Taste — it should be well seasoned and subtly sweet.

Melt the butter in a wide saucepan over medium heat until foamy. Add the sage leaves and fry for 1 min until crisp. Add the garlic, cook for 30 seconds, then pour in the cream. Simmer for 2 min and season.
Pour the cream sauce into a large baking dish. Stuff each pasta shell generously with the squash filling and nestle them into the sauce, open-side up. Scatter with extra Parmesan.
Bake for 20–25 min until bubbling and golden. Serve with a green salad.
tip: Under-cooking the pasta shells slightly before filling is essential — they continue to cook in the oven and will turn mushy if started fully cooked. Two minutes less than the packet is the rule.

name: Black Bean, Sweet Potato & Chipotle Chilli with Rice
description: Smoky chipotle paste threads through a rich, dark sauce of black beans and sweet potato — earthy, warming, and carrying just enough heat to make you reach for more. This is vegetarian chilli that doesn't feel like a compromise: thick, filling, and deeply flavoured, finished with lime and sour cream for freshness and cool.
kidNote: Use just ½ tsp chipotle paste for children and increase the tomato purée for a milder, sweeter sauce. Grated cheese on top usually seals the deal.
ingredients: 2 medium sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into 2cm cubes
sour cream, grated cheddar, fresh coriander, to serve
steps: Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Cook the onion and red pepper for 7 min until softened. Add the garlic, cumin, paprika, and chipotle paste. Cook for 2 min.
Add the sweet potato cubes and stir to coat in the spices. Cook for 3 min.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes, tomato purée, and stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 min until the sweet potato is tender.
Add the black beans and cook for a further 8–10 min until the sauce has thickened. Mash a few beans against the side of the pot to help bind the sauce.
Squeeze in the lime juice and season well with salt.
Serve over rice with sour cream, grated cheddar, and fresh coriander.
tip: Adding chipotle paste at the beginning and a final teaspoon at the end of cooking gives both depth and freshness. Taste before serving and adjust — the paste varies considerably in heat between brands.

name: Shakshuka Verde with Kale, Courgette & Feta
description: A vivid green twist on the shakshuka family — eggs baked in a herb-scented, garlicky sauce of wilted kale, courgette, and spring onion, scattered with crumbled feta and finished with a drizzle of bright herb oil. Lighter than the tomato-based original but no less satisfying, and a brilliant way to make a pan of vegetables into something genuinely special.
kidNote: Skip the chilli for children. The eggs nestled in the green sauce are fun to discover — serve with pitta or toast for scooping.
ingredients: small bunch of fresh parsley and mint
crusty bread or pitta, to serve
steps: Squeeze the grated courgette firmly in a clean tea towel to remove excess moisture — this prevents the sauce from becoming watery.
Heat the olive oil in a wide, lidded frying pan over medium heat. Cook the spring onions for 3 min, then add the garlic, chilli, cumin, and coriander. Cook for 1 min.
Add the courgette and kale in large handfuls, turning with tongs until wilted — about 4–5 min. Season well with salt, pepper, and lemon juice.
Use the back of a spoon to create eight wells in the green sauce. Crack an egg into each well.
Cover the pan and cook over medium-low heat for 6–8 min until the whites are just set and the yolks are still runny.
Scatter over the crumbled feta and fresh herbs, and serve directly from the pan with crusty bread or warm pitta.
tip: Covering the pan is the key to shakshuka — the trapped steam cooks the egg whites from above while the heat from below sets the base. Check at 6 minutes: the whites should be opaque but the yolks should wobble.

name: Smoked Salmon & Dill Frittata with Crème Fraîche
description: Delicate ribbons of smoked salmon woven through a softly set frittata scented with fresh dill and a squeeze of lemon — elegant enough for a weekend brunch but simple enough for a quick weeknight supper. A spoonful of crème fraîche on each wedge adds a cool, luxurious note that marries beautifully with the smoked fish.
kidNote: Smoked salmon is usually a hit with adventurous young eaters. Cut into small fingers for easy handling and serve the crème fraîche as a dipping sauce.
ingredients: 4 tbsp crème fraîche, plus extra to serve
small bunch of fresh dill, fronds picked
zest and juice of ½ lemon
steps: Preheat the grill to high. Beat the eggs in a large bowl, season with a little salt and plenty of black pepper. Stir in the crème fraîche, lemon zest, and half the dill.
Heat the butter and olive oil in a 26cm ovenproof frying pan over medium heat. Add the spring onions and cook for 2 min until softened.
Pour in the egg mixture and cook gently over low-medium heat, pulling the edges with a spatula and tilting the pan so uncooked egg flows to the edges, for 5–6 min until the base is set.
Scatter the smoked salmon pieces over the top, pressing them gently into the egg.
Slide under the grill for 3–4 min until the top is just set and lightly golden.
Leave to cool for 3 min. Scatter with remaining dill, a squeeze of lemon juice, and serve with extra crème fraîche and a green salad.
tip: Add the smoked salmon right at the end of hob cooking — putting it in too early toughens it. The residual heat from the egg and a brief grill is all it needs.

name: Slow-Braised Beef Short Ribs with Red Wine & Gremolata
description: Bone-in beef short ribs braised slowly in red wine and aromatic vegetables until the meat retreats from the bone in loose, molten chunks and the sauce reduces to a lacquered, deeply savoury glaze. A bright gremolata of lemon, parsley, and garlic cuts through the richness at the table — the contrast is electric. Weekend cooking that delivers extraordinary results.
kidNote: The alcohol fully cooks off during the long braise and the resulting sauce is rich and mild. Serve children with creamy mash and a small portion of the very tender beef, leaving the gremolata on the side.
ingredients: small bunch flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
creamy mashed potato or polenta, to serve
steps: Preheat the oven to 160°C/140°C fan. Pat the short ribs dry and season very generously with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy casserole over high heat. Brown the ribs in a single layer for 4–5 min per side — all four sides — until deeply seared. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium and cook the onion, carrots, and celery in the same casserole for 6 min until softened. Add the garlic and tomato purée and cook for 2 min.
Pour in the red wine and let it bubble for 3 min, scraping up all the caramelised bits from the bottom. Add the stock, thyme, and bay leaves. Return the ribs — they should be roughly half submerged.
Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and transfer to the oven. Braise for 1 hr 15 min until the meat is completely tender and yielding.

Mix together the lemon zest, minced garlic, and parsley to make the gremolata. Skim any fat from the braising liquid and season the sauce. Serve the ribs with creamy mash or polenta, sauce spooned over, and gremolata scattered on top.
tip: Thorough browning of the ribs before braising is non-negotiable — it creates the Maillard crust that enriches the entire braising liquid and gives the finished sauce its dark, complex depth.

name: Slow-Roasted Pork Shoulder with Apple, Sage & Crackling
description: Bone-in pork shoulder roasted low and slow until the meat pulls apart with a fork, the fat rendered and crisped into proper crackling, and the pan juices mingling with cider and apple into a natural, subtly sweet sauce. This is the kind of weekend cooking that fills the house with warmth for over an hour before you sit down — effortless once it's in the oven, and spectacular when it emerges.
kidNote: Pulled pork is easy for children to eat and the apple notes bring a sweetness they love. Serve in soft rolls or with mashed potato for younger eaters.
ingredients: 800g Maris Piper potatoes, cut into large chunks
steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C/200°C fan. Rub the pork skin with olive oil, sea salt flakes, fennel seeds, and smoked paprika, working it well into the scores.
Place the pork skin-side up in a large roasting tin. Roast at high heat for 20 min until the skin starts to blister and crackle.
Reduce the oven to 160°C/140°C fan. Scatter the garlic, apple quarters, and sage around the pork. Pour in the cider and 100ml water. Cover loosely with foil and return to the oven for 1 hour.
Meanwhile, parboil the potatoes for 8 min, drain, and shake in the colander to roughen the edges. Season well.
Remove the foil and add the potatoes around the pork. Return to the oven uncovered for the final 30 min until the crackling is crisp and the potatoes are golden.
Rest the pork for 15 min before pulling apart. Whisk the mustard into the pan juices and serve as a sauce alongside.
tip: Scoring the pork skin deeply — through the fat but not into the meat — and rubbing it with plenty of salt well in advance (even overnight) ensures crackling that shatters rather than bends.

name: Slow-Cooked Lamb Shoulder with Anchovies & Rosemary
description: A whole lamb shoulder studded with rosemary and anchovies — the fillets dissolving invisibly during the long roast, leaving behind a deep, savoury intensity that amplifies the lamb without ever tasting of fish. Roasted low and slow until the meat collapses at the touch of a spoon, this is the kind of weekend showpiece that turns a quiet Sunday into a celebration.
kidNote: The anchovies are completely undetectable in the finished dish — don't mention them. Serve children with mashed potato or roasted carrots alongside the very tender lamb.
ingredients: 3 sprigs fresh rosemary, broken into small sprigs
800g Maris Piper potatoes, cut into chunks
fresh mint sauce or redcurrant jelly, to serve
steps: Preheat the oven to 170°C/150°C fan. With a sharp knife, make about 20 small incisions all over the lamb shoulder. Insert a sliver of garlic, a small sprig of rosemary, and half an anchovy fillet into each incision.
Rub the lamb all over with olive oil and season generously with black pepper. Place in a large roasting tin.
Pour the wine, stock, and lemon juice around the base of the lamb. Cover the tin tightly with foil.
Roast for 1 hour, then remove the foil, add the potato chunks around the lamb, and season them well.
Return to the oven uncovered for 45 min–1 hour until the lamb is falling from the bone and the potatoes are golden.
Rest the lamb for 20 min before pulling the meat apart. Spoon the pan juices over everything and serve with mint sauce.
tip: The anchovies are not a flavour — they are a technique. Cooking them into the meat for over an hour leaves nothing fishy behind, only an amplified, meaty depth you can't quite name.

name: Classic Prawn Cocktail with Marie Rose Sauce
description: Cold, plump prawns draped in a tangy, blush-pink Marie Rose sauce — this 1970s icon endures for very good reason. The sauce, spiked with Worcestershire and a squeeze of lemon, clings to the prawns with just enough richness to satisfy. Serve in chilled glasses lined with crisp little gem for a retro starter that never fails to delight.
kidNote: Reduce or omit the Tabasco and Worcestershire sauce for a milder, sweeter version that children love.
ingredients: 1 lemon, half juiced, half cut into wedges
brown bread and butter, to serve
steps: Mix the mayonnaise, ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, Tabasco, and lemon juice together in a bowl. Season with a pinch of salt and white pepper.
Fold the prawns into the Marie Rose sauce, ensuring each one is well coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 10 minutes.
Arrange little gem leaves in the base of four chilled glasses or small bowls, then spoon the dressed cucumber over them.
Pile the dressed prawns on top and dust with a little paprika. Tuck a lemon wedge on the rim of each glass.
Serve immediately with thin slices of buttered brown bread alongside.
tip: Pat the prawns thoroughly dry before dressing — excess water dilutes the sauce and makes it watery within minutes of serving.

name: Bruschetta with Vine Tomatoes, Garlic & Basil
description: Ripe, juicy vine tomatoes tumbled with torn basil and a good pour of grassy olive oil sit atop charred, garlic-rubbed sourdough — simple enough to make in minutes, impressive enough for any table. The heat of the toast softens the garlic rub just so, releasing a gentle pungency that perfumes the whole dish. Best made with the ripest tomatoes you can find.
kidNote: Skip the raw garlic rub for children and use a light spread of garlic butter instead for a milder flavour.
ingredients: small bunch of fresh basil, leaves torn
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to drizzle
steps: Combine the chopped tomatoes, red onion, minced garlic, basil, olive oil, and red wine vinegar in a bowl. Season generously and leave to macerate for 10 minutes.
Toast or griddle the bread slices over high heat for 1-2 minutes per side until charred at the edges and crisp throughout.
While still hot, rub the cut side of the halved garlic clove firmly across one side of each slice.
Drizzle each slice with a little extra olive oil, then spoon the tomato mixture generously over the top, letting the juices soak into the bread.
Serve immediately before the bread softens.
tip: Salt the chopped tomatoes and leave them in a colander for 5 minutes to drain excess liquid — the topping becomes more concentrated and won't make the bread soggy.

name: Burrata with Roasted Cherry Tomatoes & Pesto
description: Clouds of creamy, yielding burrata sit alongside blistered, intensely sweet roasted cherry tomatoes, pooled in verdant pesto and scattered with flaky sea salt. When you break the burrata open, the rich, milky cream spills across the plate in the most satisfying way. Serve with warm focaccia for one of the most effortlessly elegant starters imaginable.
kidNote: Children usually adore the mild, milky burrata — simply leave out the pesto and offer just the cheese with torn bread.
ingredients: 4 tbsp fresh green pesto (shop-bought is fine)
flaky sea salt and black pepper
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Toss the cherry tomatoes with 2 tbsp olive oil, season well, and roast on a baking tray for 15 minutes until blistered and collapsed.
Spread a spoonful of pesto across the base of each serving plate.
Place one burrata ball in the centre of each plate, then arrange the warm roasted tomatoes alongside.
Drizzle with the remaining olive oil and balsamic glaze, then scatter with fresh basil leaves.
Finish with a generous pinch of flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper. Serve at once with warm focaccia.
tip: Remove the burrata from the fridge 20 minutes before serving — cold burrata is dense; at room temperature it blooms open beautifully when cut.

name: Smooth Chicken Liver Pâté with Toasted Brioche
description: Velvety, butter-enriched chicken liver pâté with a whisper of brandy and fresh thyme spreads like silk across warm, golden brioche toast. The livers are cooked briefly — just enough to lose their rawness — so they remain blush-pink inside, yielding the smoothest, most delicate result. A proper restaurant starter that costs almost nothing to make at home.
kidNote: Serve children a thin spread on plain toast soldiers; the mild, buttery flavour is usually well received, but keep portions small.
ingredients: cornichons and dressed leaves, to serve
steps: Melt 50g of the butter in a frying pan over medium heat. Add the shallot and garlic and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and translucent.
Turn the heat up to medium-high, add the chicken livers and thyme, and cook for 3 minutes, turning once — the livers should be golden outside but still slightly pink within.
Pour in the brandy carefully and let it bubble for 1 minute to cook off the alcohol. Remove from the heat and discard the thyme sprigs.
Transfer the contents of the pan to a food processor. Add the remaining 100g butter and the double cream, and blitz until completely smooth. Season well with salt and white pepper.
Pass through a fine sieve into ramekins for the silkiest result. Press a piece of cling film onto the surface and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight.
Serve with thick slices of toasted brioche, cornichons, and lightly dressed leaves.
tip: The key to ultra-smooth pâté is passing it through a fine-mesh sieve after blending — this removes any fibrous bits and produces a restaurant-quality texture.

name: Smoked Salmon Blinis with Crème Fraîche & Dill
description: Buckwheat-tinged blinis, tender and slightly spongy, carry silky ribbons of smoked salmon and cool, dill-flecked crème fraîche into every elegant mouthful. A squeeze of lemon and a few capers cut through the richness, making each little bite perfectly balanced. These have the feel of a proper celebration starter but come together in under half an hour.
kidNote: Children tend to enjoy these with just crème fraîche and mild smoked salmon — skip the capers and horseradish for younger palates.
ingredients: 1 tbsp butter, melted, plus extra for cooking
steps: Whisk together the flour, yeast, and salt in a bowl. Add the egg and melted butter, then gradually whisk in the warm milk until you have a smooth batter. Cover and rest for 20 minutes until slightly puffy.
Stir the horseradish sauce, if using, into the crème fraîche with a few fronds of dill and a squeeze of lemon juice. Season lightly and refrigerate.

Heat a non-stick frying pan over medium heat and brush with a little butter. Drop heaped tablespoons of batter into the pan and cook for 1-2 minutes until bubbles form on the surface, then flip and cook for 1 minute more. Keep warm in a low oven.
Arrange the warm blinis on a platter. Top each with a small spoonful of the crème fraîche mixture and a folded ribbon of smoked salmon.
Finish with a few capers, a frond of dill, and a small squeeze of lemon. Serve immediately.
tip: Don't flip the blinis until bubbles have appeared across the whole surface — patience at this stage ensures an evenly cooked, fluffy result rather than a doughy centre.

name: Baked Camembert with Honey, Rosemary & Walnuts
description: A whole Camembert, slashed and stuffed with rosemary and garlic, emerges from the oven molten and fragrant, its rind barely containing a river of molten, earthy cheese. A drizzle of warm honey and a handful of toasted walnuts add sweet crunch that plays beautifully against the funky, creamy interior. Tear in with crusty bread and watch the table fall blissfully silent.
kidNote: Children love dipping bread into melted cheese — skip the walnuts for younger kids and serve with mild crackers or breadsticks.
ingredients: 1 x 250g Camembert in a wooden box
crusty bread or breadsticks, to serve
steps: Preheat the oven to 190°C/170°C fan. Remove the Camembert from its packaging, return it to the base of the wooden box, and place on a baking tray.
Using a small knife, score the top of the rind in a crosshatch pattern. Tuck the garlic slices and rosemary sprigs into the cuts.
Drizzle 1 tbsp of the honey over the top and season with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Bake for 15-18 minutes until the cheese is completely melted and bubbling.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry frying pan with the olive oil for 2-3 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Remove the Camembert from the oven, scatter over the toasted walnuts, and drizzle with the remaining honey. Serve immediately with plenty of crusty bread for dipping.
tip: Wrap the wooden box in a double layer of foil before baking — this prevents the box from scorching and contains any cheese that bubbles over the rind.

name: Beetroot & Goat's Cheese Salad with Walnuts
description: Jewel-bright roasted beetroot, its earthy sweetness intensified by the oven, sits against cool, crumbling goat's cheese and bitter watercress in a deeply satisfying contrast of colour and flavour. A honey and balsamic dressing threads through the whole salad with a glossy, lightly tart finish. This is the kind of starter that makes people think you've spent the afternoon in the kitchen.
kidNote: Serve children a simpler plate of just the beetroot and mild cheese without the watercress or vinegar dressing — a drizzle of honey is usually a hit.
ingredients: 500g cooked beetroot (not in vinegar), cut into wedges
steps: Whisk together the olive oil, balsamic vinegar, honey, and Dijon mustard in a small bowl. Season with salt and pepper to make the dressing.
Arrange the watercress or rocket across a large serving platter or divide between four plates.
Scatter the beetroot wedges over the leaves, then dot generously with crumbled goat's cheese.
Scatter over the toasted walnuts and drizzle the dressing evenly across the whole salad.
Serve immediately at room temperature — the slightly warm beetroot against the cool cheese is part of the appeal.
tip: Roast raw beetroot yourself for far superior flavour: wrap in foil with a splash of olive oil and roast at 200°C for 45-60 minutes until tender throughout.

name: Crispy Arancini with Mozzarella & Tomato Sauce
description: Golden, shatteringly crisp rice balls conceal a molten heart of mozzarella that stretches dramatically on the pull — arancini in their full, magnificent form. The risotto base is seasoned with parmesan and a whisper of saffron, lending the crumb a deep, savoury richness. Serve with a sharp tomato dipping sauce and watch them disappear.
kidNote: Children adore the melted cheese centre — make them smaller (golf ball size) for easier eating and serve with ketchup instead of the tomato sauce.
ingredients: 300g cold leftover risotto (or cook 200g arborio rice with 600ml stock)
125g mozzarella ball, cut into 12 small cubes
steps: Make the tomato sauce first: fry the garlic in olive oil for 1 minute, add the chopped tomatoes, chilli, and sugar, and simmer for 15 minutes. Season and keep warm.

Mix the cold risotto with the parmesan and season well. With damp hands, take a golf-ball-sized portion, flatten slightly, press a cube of mozzarella into the centre, and roll firmly into a smooth ball. Repeat to make 12.
Set up a breading station: flour in one bowl, beaten egg in another, breadcrumbs in a third. Roll each arancino in flour, dip in egg, then roll generously in breadcrumbs. Press the crumbs on firmly.
Heat 8cm of oil in a deep saucepan to 175°C. Fry the arancini in batches of 3-4 for 3-4 minutes, turning gently, until deeply golden all over. Drain on kitchen paper.
Serve hot with the tomato dipping sauce alongside.
tip: The risotto must be completely cold and stiff before rolling — warm risotto is too soft to hold its shape and will fall apart in the oil. Chilling overnight is ideal.

name: Melon, Prosciutto & Burrata with Mint Oil
description: Silk-thin prosciutto draped over sweet cantaloupe melon alongside pillowy burrata and a vibrant mint oil — this is summer assembled on a plate, no cooking required. The salty, nutty cured ham and the cool, fragrant melon are one of the great flavour marriages in all of Italian cuisine, and the fresh mint oil lifts the whole dish with a bright, herbal note. Ready in ten minutes and fit for any occasion.
kidNote: Children enjoy the sweet melon and mild mozzarella — simply leave off the prosciutto or serve it on the side for those who prefer it.
ingredients: 1 ripe cantaloupe melon, halved, seeds removed, sliced into wedges
small bunch of fresh mint, leaves picked
flaky sea salt and black pepper
steps: Blitz the mint leaves with the olive oil and white wine vinegar using a stick blender or small food processor until you have a vibrant green oil. Season lightly.
Arrange the melon wedges across a large serving platter, then drape the prosciutto slices loosely between and over the melon.
Tear the burrata and arrange the pieces across the platter.
Drizzle generously with the mint oil and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and a crack of black pepper.
Serve immediately, at room temperature, with bread to mop up the juices if desired.
tip: The melon must be fully ripe for this dish to sing — a ripe cantaloupe should smell intensely sweet and fragrant at the stem end.

name: Crab on Toast with Lemon, Chilli & Avocado
description: Sweet, fresh white crab meat, brightened with lemon and a whisper of chilli, sits on a layer of cool, creamy avocado atop thick slices of sourdough toast — a starter that feels genuinely luxurious. The contrast between the yielding avocado, the delicate sweetness of the crab, and the char of the bread is deeply satisfying.
kidNote: Use half the amount of chilli or omit it entirely for children, who usually enjoy the sweet, mild crab on buttered toast just as much.
ingredients: 200g fresh or good-quality tinned white crab meat
1 red chilli, finely chopped (seeds removed for less heat)
small bunch of fresh chives, snipped
steps: Scoop the avocado flesh into a bowl, add half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and roughly mash to a textured purée.

Pick through the crab meat carefully for any stray shell. Combine the crab with the crème fraîche, lemon zest, remaining lemon juice, most of the chilli, and half the chives. Season with salt and white pepper.
Toast or griddle the sourdough slices until golden and crisp on both sides.
Spread each slice generously with the avocado mash, then top with a pile of the dressed crab.
Finish with the remaining chilli, the rest of the chives, and a drizzle of olive oil. Serve immediately.
tip: Fresh dressed crab from the fishmonger gives a far superior result to tinned — the natural sweetness of the white meat needs very little adornment.

name: Potato Dauphinoise with Gruyère & Thyme
description: Paper-thin slices of potato, slow-cooked in garlicky cream until silky and yielding, crowned with a crust of golden, bubbling Gruyère — this is the pinnacle of the potato side dish. Each layer absorbs the cream and releases a gentle starchiness that makes the whole dish impossibly unctuous. Rich, warming, and deeply comforting, it belongs alongside roast lamb, beef, or anything that needs something truly magnificent next to it.
kidNote: Children adore this — the creamy, cheesy potatoes are universally popular. Just ensure the slices are well-cooked all the way through so they're not too firm.
steps: Preheat the oven to 170°C/150°C fan. Butter a large ovenproof gratin dish generously.
Combine the cream, milk, garlic, thyme leaves, nutmeg, salt, and pepper in a saucepan and warm over low heat for 5 minutes. Do not boil.
Using a mandoline or very sharp knife, slice the potatoes as thinly as possible (2-3mm). Do not rinse — the starch is essential for thickening.
Layer the potato slices overlapping in the prepared dish. Pour the warm cream mixture through a sieve over the potatoes, pressing them down so they're just submerged.

Scatter the grated Gruyère evenly over the top. Cover tightly with foil and bake for 55 minutes, then remove the foil and bake for a further 20-25 minutes until deeply golden and a knife slides through without resistance.
Leave to rest for 10 minutes before serving — this helps the layers set so the dish cuts cleanly.
tip: Adding the potatoes raw to the infused cream allows the starch to leach out slowly, creating a far richer, more set result than blanching first.

name: Crispy Smashed Potatoes with Garlic Herb Butter
description: Boiled baby potatoes smashed flat and roasted until their edges are lacquer-crisp and their centres fluffy and steaming, then drenched in a garlicky, herby butter — these are the potato side dish that everyone fights over. The dual-cooking method gives you the best of both worlds: a crunchy golden crust with a cloud-like interior.
kidNote: Children love the crispy edges — these are far more exciting than ordinary boiled or roast potatoes, and the buttery flavour appeals to all ages.
ingredients: small bunch of flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
flaky sea salt and black pepper
steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C/200°C fan. Boil the potatoes in well-salted water for 18-20 minutes until completely tender. Drain and steam dry for 5 minutes.

Transfer the potatoes to a large roasting tin, spacing them well apart. Use the base of a glass or your palm to press each potato flat until the skin splits and the flesh spreads out to roughly 1.5cm thick.
Drizzle the smashed potatoes generously with olive oil, season with salt and pepper, and roast for 25-30 minutes until the edges are deeply golden and shatteringly crisp.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook for 1-2 minutes until fragrant but not coloured. Stir in the thyme and most of the parsley.
Transfer the crispy potatoes to a warm serving dish and immediately pour the garlic herb butter all over them. Scatter with the remaining parsley and flaky salt. Serve at once.
tip: The steam-dry step after boiling is crucial — wet potatoes won't crisp in the oven. Let them sit in the colander for a full 5 minutes.

name: Hasselback Potatoes with Soured Cream & Chives
description: Potatoes sliced almost through into paper-thin fans, brushed repeatedly with butter as they roast, emerge from the oven with impossibly crispy edges and a soft, yielding centre — each fin catching butter and herbs between its layers. The visual drama alone makes them worth the small effort, and the cool, herb-flecked soured cream alongside is the perfect counterpoint.
kidNote: Children enjoy these for their interactive look — let them add their own soured cream and chive toppings at the table.
ingredients: 8 medium Maris Piper potatoes (about 150g each), scrubbed
flaky sea salt and black pepper
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Place each potato on a chopping board between two wooden spoon handles. Slice at 3mm intervals along the length of each potato — the spoon handles act as guides so you don't cut all the way through.
Mix the melted butter, olive oil, garlic, and thyme together. Place the potatoes in a roasting tin, brush generously with the butter mixture, letting it seep into the cuts. Season well.
Roast for 40 minutes, then remove and baste again with the butter mixture, gently fanning the cuts open slightly. Return to the oven for a further 25-30 minutes until golden and crisp.
Meanwhile, mix the soured cream with the chives and season with salt.
Serve the hasselback potatoes hot from the oven with a generous spoonful of chive soured cream alongside and a final pinch of flaky salt.
tip: Basting twice during cooking is what gives hasselbacks their signature layered crunch — don't skip the second brush at the 40-minute mark.

name: Roasted Tenderstem Broccoli with Chilli & Parmesan
description: Slender tenderstem broccoli spears, roasted at high heat until their tips are frizzled and their stalks tender-crisp, finished with a shower of parmesan and a kick of chilli. The high-heat roasting brings out a nutty, almost caramelised quality that steaming simply cannot replicate. Ready in twenty minutes and pairs with almost everything.
kidNote: For younger children, reduce or omit the chilli flakes and serve with a squeeze of lemon and a little milder cheese such as cheddar.
ingredients: flaky sea salt and black pepper
steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C/200°C fan. Spread the tenderstem broccoli across a large baking sheet in a single layer — don't crowd the pan or it will steam rather than roast.
Drizzle with olive oil, scatter over the garlic slices and chilli flakes, and season generously. Toss to coat.
Roast for 12-15 minutes until the stems are tender and the floret tips are golden and slightly crispy.
Remove from the oven and immediately scatter with the grated parmesan and lemon zest, allowing the residual heat to melt the cheese.
Transfer to a warm serving platter and serve at once.
tip: Dry the broccoli thoroughly after washing — any moisture on the surface will steam the spears and prevent the caramelisation that makes this dish so good.

name: Honey-Roasted Carrots with Cumin & Fresh Herbs
description: Whole carrots roasted until their natural sugars concentrate and caramelise under a glaze of warm honey and aromatic cumin — these are gloriously transformed from the ordinary to the exceptional. A scatter of fresh herbs and a squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the sweetness and adds a fragrant brightness. An elegant side that pairs with everything from roast lamb to grilled fish.
kidNote: Children often prefer carrots when they're sweet and soft like these — the honey glaze makes them a much easier sell than steamed or boiled versions.
ingredients: 600g medium carrots, peeled and halved lengthways
small bunch of fresh coriander or flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Toss the carrots with olive oil, honey, cumin, ground coriander, and the unpeeled garlic cloves. Season well.
Spread in a single layer on a large roasting tin. Roast for 20 minutes, then turn the carrots and return to the oven for a further 12-15 minutes until caramelised and tender.
Remove the garlic cloves and squeeze over the lemon juice.
Transfer to a warm serving platter and scatter with the fresh herbs.
Serve immediately while the glaze is still sticky and fragrant.
tip: Use carrots of similar size so they cook evenly — if some are thicker, split them lengthways once more so every piece caramelises at the same rate.

name: Classic Caesar Salad with Soft-Boiled Egg
description: Crisp romaine lettuce coated in a deeply savoury, anchovy-spiked Caesar dressing, studded with golden croutons and showered in parmesan — this is one of the great salads of the world. The addition of a perfectly soft-boiled egg elevates it into something almost substantial, and the dressing, garlicky and umami-rich, clings to every leaf.
kidNote: Serve children with a lighter dressing (increase the lemon, reduce the anchovy) and make sure the eggs are cooked through.
ingredients: 2 romaine lettuces, outer leaves removed, torn
4 thick slices ciabatta or sourdough, torn into chunks
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Toss the bread chunks with olive oil and season, then spread on a baking sheet and bake for 10-12 minutes until golden and crisp.
Bring a pan of water to a boil, lower in the eggs, and cook for exactly 7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Transfer immediately to iced water for 3 minutes, then peel.
Make the dressing: pound the anchovies and garlic to a paste using a pestle and mortar. Beat in the mayonnaise, lemon juice, Dijon, and grated parmesan. Season well with pepper.
Add enough dressing to coat the romaine leaves thoroughly — start with half and add more to taste. Toss well.
Arrange on a platter, scatter over the croutons and shaved parmesan, halve the soft-boiled eggs and nestle them among the leaves. Serve immediately.
tip: Make the dressing up to 48 hours ahead and refrigerate — it deepens considerably overnight and the garlic mellows beautifully.

name: Creamy Cauliflower Cheese with Mature Cheddar
description: Tender cauliflower florets blanketed in a thick, golden béchamel sauce loaded with sharp mature Cheddar and a whisper of mustard — baked until the top is bubbling, bronzed, and irresistible. The sauce is unashamedly rich and clinging, the kind that pools in the base of the dish and gets scraped clean with a spoon. This is British comfort food at its very finest.
kidNote: This is a universally loved children's dish — the cheese sauce makes even the most reluctant vegetable-avoiders come back for seconds.
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Cook the cauliflower in a large pan of well-salted boiling water for 6-8 minutes until just tender. Drain thoroughly and tip into a large ovenproof dish.
Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir in the flour and cook for 1-2 minutes, stirring constantly, to form a smooth paste. Remove from the heat.

Gradually whisk in the milk, a splash at a time at first, then in larger additions, until you have a smooth, lump-free sauce. Return to medium heat and cook, stirring, until thickened — about 5 minutes.
Remove from the heat, stir in 100g of the Cheddar, the mustard, a grating of nutmeg, and season well. Pour the sauce evenly over the cauliflower.
Scatter the remaining Cheddar and the breadcrumbs (if using) over the top. Bake for 20-25 minutes until golden and bubbling. Serve hot.
tip: Add the milk to the roux off the heat and in small additions at first — this virtually eliminates lumps without needing to whisk frantically over the heat.

name: Creamed Spinach with Nutmeg & Garlic
description: Bags of fresh baby spinach wilted down and stirred through a silky, garlic-scented cream sauce with a warming grate of nutmeg — a side dish of effortless elegance that pairs magnificently with steak, fish, or roast chicken. The spinach collapses dramatically in volume, concentrating its flavour into something altogether more refined. Rich but not heavy, on the table in a quarter of an hour.
kidNote: Children who baulk at plain spinach are often won over by the creamy sauce — start with a small portion and increase the nutmeg very sparingly.
steps: Melt the butter in your largest saucepan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the spinach in large handfuls, turning with tongs, allowing each batch to wilt before adding the next. This will take 3-4 minutes in total.
Tip the wilted spinach into a colander and press firmly with the back of a spoon to extract as much water as possible.
Return the pan to medium heat, pour in the cream, and let it bubble for 2-3 minutes until slightly reduced. Add the spinach back in and toss to coat.
Stir in the parmesan, grate over nutmeg generously, and season with salt and white pepper. Serve immediately.
tip: Squeezing the spinach dry is the single most important step — excess water will split the cream sauce and produce a thin, watery result.

name: Honey-Glazed Roasted Parsnips with Sage
description: Wedges of parsnip roasted in goose fat until their cut sides caramelise deeply, finished with a lick of warm honey and crispy fried sage leaves — this is the finest thing to do with a parsnip. The natural sweetness of the parsnip intensifies beautifully in the oven, and the sage adds an aromatic, almost festive note that makes these a natural partner for any roast.
kidNote: The honey glaze makes parsnips very appealing to children — roast them a little longer until very soft in the centre if your children prefer a less firm texture.
ingredients: 600g parsnips, peeled, halved lengthways and quartered if large
3 tbsp goose fat or olive oil
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Toss the parsnips in goose fat (or olive oil), season generously, and spread in a single layer on a large roasting tin.
Roast for 25 minutes, then turn them and drizzle the honey over the tops. Return to the oven for a further 12-15 minutes until deeply golden and sticky.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a small frying pan over high heat. When it foams, add the sage leaves and fry for 30-60 seconds until crisp. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Transfer the glazed parsnips to a warm serving dish and scatter over the crispy sage leaves and fresh thyme.
Serve at once while the glaze is still sticky and shining.
tip: Parboil the parsnips for 5 minutes before roasting if your oven runs cool — this guarantees a fluffy interior to contrast with the caramelised exterior.

name: Roasted Garlic & Herb Flatbreads
description: Pillowy, handmade flatbreads cooked directly in a hot griddle pan until they blister and char in places, then brushed immediately with fragrant roasted garlic butter and scattered with fresh herbs. The slightly charred exterior gives a gentle smokiness that shop-bought garlic bread simply cannot replicate. Serve alongside soups, stews, curries, or any dish that deserves something special for dipping.
kidNote: Children love tearing and dipping these — reduce the garlic slightly for younger palates and skip the chilli flakes if preferred.
ingredients: 300g self-raising flour, plus extra for dusting
small bunch of flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
steps: Mix the flour, baking powder, and salt in a large bowl. Add the yoghurt and mix to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface and knead briefly until smooth. Divide into 4 equal balls.
Roll each ball out on a lightly floured surface to approximately 3mm thickness and an oval shape.
Heat a griddle or heavy frying pan over high heat until very hot. Cook each flatbread for 2-3 minutes per side until charred spots appear and the bread puffs slightly.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a small pan, add the garlic and chilli flakes if using, and cook for 1-2 minutes over low heat. Remove from heat and stir in the parsley.
As each flatbread comes off the griddle, brush immediately and generously with the garlic herb butter. Stack them wrapped in a clean tea towel to keep warm. Serve at once.
tip: The griddle must be smoking hot before the first flatbread goes in — a properly hot surface creates those essential charred blisters.

name: Roasted Asparagus with Lemon & Almonds
description: Bright green asparagus spears, roasted at high heat until their tips are just beginning to colour and their stalks have that wonderful snap-and-give texture, finished with toasted flaked almonds and a shower of lemon zest. This is spring on a plate — light, verdant, and ready in under twenty minutes. The almonds add a buttery crunch that complements the asparagus perfectly.
kidNote: Many children enjoy asparagus when it's well seasoned and roasted rather than boiled — serve without the almonds if there are nut allergies.
ingredients: 500g asparagus spears, woody ends snapped off
flaky sea salt and black pepper
steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C/200°C fan. Arrange the asparagus in a single layer on a large baking sheet. Drizzle with olive oil, season well, and toss to coat.
Roast for 10-12 minutes until the spears are tender and the tips are just beginning to colour.
Meanwhile, toast the flaked almonds in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2-3 minutes until golden. Add the butter and let it foam, then remove from the heat immediately.
Transfer the asparagus to a warm serving platter, squeeze over the lemon juice, and scatter with the toasted almonds and the lemon zest.
Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and serve immediately.
tip: To find the natural snap point on asparagus, hold each spear at both ends and bend gently — it will break right where the woody base meets the tender stalk.

name: Classic Coleslaw with Apple & Poppy Seeds
description: Crisp, finely shredded white cabbage and carrot tossed in a lightly creamy, tangy dressing brightened with sharp apple and the subtle crunch of poppy seeds — coleslaw taken just far enough beyond the classic to make it feel interesting. Cool, crunchy, and refreshing, it cuts through rich BBQ meats and fried food brilliantly. This version keeps the dressing light so the vegetables stay the star.
kidNote: Children usually love coleslaw — reduce the vinegar slightly for a milder, sweeter version and grate the vegetables more finely for easier eating.
ingredients: 1 Granny Smith apple, cored and cut into thin matchsticks
steps: Combine the shredded cabbage, grated carrot, and apple matchsticks in a large bowl.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the mayonnaise, Greek yoghurt, cider vinegar, Dijon mustard, and caster sugar until smooth. Season with salt and white pepper.
Pour the dressing over the vegetables and toss thoroughly to ensure everything is well coated.
Scatter in the poppy seeds and toss once more.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before serving to allow the flavours to meld and the cabbage to soften slightly.
tip: Salt the shredded cabbage lightly and leave it in a colander for 20 minutes before using — this draws out excess moisture and prevents the coleslaw from becoming watery as it sits.

name: Sticky Toffee Pudding with Hot Butterscotch Sauce
description: Deeply dark, moist date sponge with a fudgy, almost gingerbread-like quality, drowned in a glossy butterscotch sauce that smells like caramelised sugar and vanilla — this is Britain's most beloved dessert, and with good reason. The dates melt invisibly into the batter, adding a deep, fruity richness without a trace of date-flavour complaint from the uninitiated. Served with a scoop of vanilla ice cream and a generous pour of sauce, it is pure, unapologetic comfort.
kidNote: An all-round children's favourite — the rich toffee sauce is irresistible. Make sure the sauce is not scalding hot before serving to younger children.
steps: Preheat the oven to 180°C/160°C fan. Grease a 20cm square baking tin. Place the dates and boiling water in a bowl, stir in the bicarbonate of soda, and leave for 10 minutes until the dates soften. Blitz to a rough purée.
Beat the butter and sugar together until light and fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then fold in the flour. Stir in the date purée and vanilla extract until just combined.
Pour into the prepared tin and bake for 30-35 minutes until risen and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.

While the pudding bakes, make the sauce: melt the butter and sugar together in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves. Add the cream and vanilla, bring to a gentle boil, and cook for 2-3 minutes until thickened. Add the pinch of salt.

Remove the pudding from the oven and immediately prick all over with a skewer. Pour a third of the sauce over the hot pudding and leave to soak for 5 minutes before cutting into portions. Serve with the remaining sauce poured over and vanilla ice cream alongside.
tip: The pudding improves markedly if made a day ahead and reheated, covered in foil, at 160°C for 15 minutes — the flavours deepen overnight and the texture becomes even more fudgy.

name: Individual Chocolate Fondants with Vanilla Ice Cream
description: Four dark, glossy little puddings that appear fully set until the moment you break through their crust and a river of warm molten chocolate flows onto the plate — the fondant is theatre and substance in equal measure. Made with good dark chocolate and very little else, these are deeply intense and luxurious. They can be prepared ahead and baked from cold, making them perfect for dinner parties.
kidNote: Children adore the 'lava' effect — use milk chocolate instead of dark for a sweeter, less intense result.
ingredients: 150g good-quality dark chocolate (70% cocoa), broken up
150g unsalted butter, diced, plus extra for greasing
good vanilla ice cream, to serve
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Butter four 200ml individual pudding moulds or ramekins generously, then dust with cocoa powder, tapping out any excess.
Melt the chocolate and butter together in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, stirring until smooth. Remove from the heat and leave to cool for 5 minutes.
In a large bowl, whisk together the eggs, egg yolks, and caster sugar with an electric whisk for about 3 minutes until pale, thick, and doubled in volume.
Gently fold the chocolate mixture into the egg mixture, then sift in the flour and fold in until just combined. Divide between the prepared moulds.

At this point you can refrigerate the moulds for up to 24 hours. Bake straight from the fridge for 14 minutes (or 12 minutes if cooking immediately) until the edges are set but the centre still wobbles distinctly. Run a knife around the edge of each fondant, invert onto a warm plate, and leave for 10 seconds before lifting the mould. Serve immediately with ice cream.
tip: Baking time is everything — 14 minutes produces a perfectly flowing centre. Test your oven with one fondant first, as ovens vary.

name: Classic Tiramisu with Espresso & Marsala
description: Layers of coffee-soaked sponge fingers and cloud-like mascarpone cream, dusted with a thick cloak of dark cocoa — the Italian dessert that has conquered the world's restaurants. The mascarpone cream is beaten with egg yolks and enriched with Marsala wine, giving it a depth and silkiness that surpasses anything pre-made. Best chilled overnight, when every layer melds into harmonious, coffee-scented perfection.
kidNote: Make a child-friendly version by substituting the espresso with diluted hot chocolate and omitting the Marsala — the texture and fun of the layers remain entirely intact.
ingredients: 3 tbsp Marsala wine or dark rum
200ml strong espresso or very strong coffee, cooled
3 tbsp dark cocoa powder, for dusting
steps: Whisk the egg yolks with the caster sugar until very pale, thick, and ribbon-like — about 5 minutes with an electric whisk. Beat in the mascarpone and Marsala until smooth.
In a clean bowl with clean beaters, whisk the egg whites to stiff peaks. Fold carefully into the mascarpone mixture in two additions, keeping as much air as possible.

Mix the espresso with 1 tbsp of the Marsala in a shallow bowl. Working quickly, dip each sponge finger briefly — just 1-2 seconds per side — and arrange a layer in the base of a medium dish or four individual glasses.
Spread half the mascarpone cream over the soaked biscuits. Add another layer of dipped sponge fingers, then top with the remaining cream, smoothing the surface.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or ideally overnight. Dust generously with cocoa powder through a fine sieve just before serving.
tip: Dip the sponge fingers briefly — just long enough to absorb the coffee without becoming waterlogged. Soggy biscuits collapse into mush; a light dip leaves them with a pleasing, slightly firm texture.

name: Eton Mess with Strawberries & Whipped Cream
description: Broken meringue shards, clouds of softly whipped cream, and jewel-red macerated strawberries tumbled together in the most glorious, unconstrained fashion — Eton Mess is the dessert that celebrates imperfection and tastes all the better for it. The strawberries are briefly macerated with a little sugar and lemon to draw out their juices, which bleed beautifully into the cream. This is summer in a bowl, assembled in minutes.
kidNote: Children adore assembling their own Eton mess at the table — set out bowls of meringue, cream, and strawberries and let them build their own version.
ingredients: 500g ripe strawberries, hulled and roughly sliced
steps: Toss the strawberries with the icing sugar and lemon juice in a bowl. Leave to macerate for 15 minutes until the juices run. Lightly crush a quarter of them with a fork to create a natural sauce.
Whip the double cream with the caster sugar and vanilla extract to soft, billowing peaks — stop while it still falls in gentle folds.
Roughly break the meringue nests into large, irregular shards.
Fold the strawberries (and all their juices), two-thirds of the meringue, and the whipped cream together with just a few strokes — the beauty is in the uneven ripples of pink and white.
Spoon into glasses or bowls and top with the remaining meringue pieces. Serve immediately.
tip: Assemble this dish right before serving — if it sits for more than 20 minutes, the meringue begins to dissolve into the cream and loses its wonderful textural contrast.

name: Lemon Posset with Shortbread Biscuits
description: Three ingredients — cream, sugar, and lemon — transform by culinary alchemy into a perfectly set, trembling, silk-smooth cream with a bright, sharp citrus hit that clears the palate as effectively as any sorbet. No gelatine, no baking, no fuss: the acid from the lemon alone causes the cream to set. Paired with crumbly, buttery shortbread, it is a masterclass in restraint.
kidNote: Children enjoy the smooth, creamy texture — reduce the lemon juice slightly if they find the sharpness too intense, and serve with a few fresh berries alongside.
ingredients: 3 lemons, zested and juiced (you need 100ml juice)
steps: If making the shortbread, rub the butter into the flour and sugar until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs, then press into a rectangle, cut into fingers, and bake at 180°C for 15-18 minutes until pale golden. Cool completely.
Combine the cream, sugar, and lemon zest in a saucepan. Bring to a gentle boil, stirring to dissolve the sugar, then simmer for exactly 3 minutes, stirring.
Remove from the heat and stir in the lemon juice. Leave to cool for 5 minutes, then pour through a fine sieve into four small glasses or ramekins.
Leave to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate, uncovered, for at least 3 hours or overnight until set.
Serve chilled with shortbread fingers alongside.
tip: The exact lemon juice quantity matters — too little and the posset won't set; too much and it will curdle slightly. Measure 100ml precisely with a jug.

name: Classic Apple Crumble with Vanilla Custard
description: Tender, cinnamon-spiced Bramley apples bubbling beneath a shaggy, golden oat-flecked crumble topping that shatters at the touch of a spoon — the apple crumble is Britain's most-requested home dessert. The contrast between the sharp, collapsing fruit and the sandy, buttery crust is one of food's great textural pleasures. Poured custard is non-negotiable.
kidNote: A guaranteed children's favourite — for extra appeal, let them scatter the crumble topping on themselves before it goes in the oven.
ingredients: 700g Bramley apples, peeled, cored and roughly chopped
ready-made or homemade vanilla custard, to serve
steps: Preheat the oven to 190°C/170°C fan. Place the apples, caster sugar, cinnamon, and water in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the apples begin to break down. Tip into a 1.5-litre ovenproof dish.
Make the crumble: rub the cold butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips until the mixture resembles rough, uneven breadcrumbs — some larger lumps are desirable.
Stir in the demerara sugar and rolled oats. The mixture should clump loosely when squeezed.
Scatter the crumble evenly over the apple mixture without pressing it down — keeping it loose allows steam to escape and the surface to crisp properly.
Bake for 30-35 minutes until the topping is deeply golden and the fruit is bubbling up around the edges. Leave to stand for 5 minutes before serving with warm vanilla custard.
tip: Use cold butter from the fridge and handle the crumble mixture as little as possible — warm butter from overworking creates a compact, dense topping that bakes soggy rather than shatteringly crisp.

name: Vanilla Panna Cotta with Raspberry Coulis
description: Ivory-pale, trembling panna cotta with the scent of vanilla bean and the delicate give of barely-set cream — Italian elegance in its purest form. Turned out onto a plate, it wobbles with fragile intention before being draped in a vivid scarlet raspberry coulis that bleeds across the white surface like a painting. Deceptively simple to make, it requires only good ingredients and patience while it sets.
kidNote: Children love the wobbly, creamy texture — the raspberry coulis provides natural sweetness that appeals to all ages. Use shop-bought coulis for ease.
ingredients: 1 vanilla pod, split, or 2 tsp vanilla extract
steps: Sprinkle the gelatine over the cold water in a small bowl and leave to bloom for 5 minutes.

Combine the cream, milk, sugar, and vanilla pod (or extract) in a saucepan. Heat gently, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is just below boiling. Remove from the heat and discard the vanilla pod.
Add the bloomed gelatine to the hot cream mixture and stir until completely dissolved. Strain through a fine sieve into a jug.
Lightly oil four 150ml dariole moulds or ramekins. Pour in the cream mixture and leave to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight until firmly set.

For the coulis, blend the raspberries with icing sugar and lemon juice, then pass through a fine sieve. To unmould, run a knife around the edge, hold a plate over the top, and invert firmly. Spoon coulis around each panna cotta and serve.
tip: The gelatine quantity here gives a just-set wobble — perfect for turning out. If serving in glasses (no unmoulding needed), reduce the gelatine to 2 tsp for an even more silken result.

name: Banoffee Pie with Salted Toffee Sauce
description: A crumbly biscuit base, a thick layer of dark, sticky salted toffee, sliced ripe bananas, and a cloud of cold whipped cream dusted with chocolate — banoffee pie is one of those desserts that asks very little of the cook and gives enormously in return. The combination of salt, caramel, banana, and cream is so perfectly calibrated that it's essentially impossible not to want a second slice.
kidNote: Children adore banoffee pie — make individual versions in glasses for a fun, spill-proof presentation that they can carry to the table themselves.
ingredients: 300ml double cream, whipped to soft peaks
steps: Crush the digestive biscuits to fine crumbs. Mix with the melted butter and press firmly into the base and sides of a 20cm loose-bottomed tart tin. Refrigerate for 20 minutes.

Make the toffee: melt the butter and sugar together in a heavy-based saucepan over medium heat. Add the condensed milk and cook, stirring constantly, for 5-7 minutes until the mixture thickens and turns a deep golden caramel colour. Stir in the flaky salt. Pour over the biscuit base and refrigerate for 1 hour until set.
Arrange the sliced bananas over the set toffee layer.
Spread or pipe the whipped cream generously over the bananas.
Finish with a generous grating of dark chocolate directly over the cream. Slice and serve chilled.
tip: Stir the condensed milk mixture constantly throughout cooking and never leave it unattended — the sugars can catch and burn in seconds, turning the toffee bitter.

name: Crème Brûlée with Vanilla & Orange Zest
description: Beneath a caramel shell that yields with a satisfying crack lies one of the finest creations in the French pastry canon — a cool, trembling, vanilla-scented custard of extraordinary richness, perfumed here with a hint of orange zest. The contrast between the glassy, brittle sugar crust and the silken cream beneath is what makes crème brûlée so enduringly, compulsively satisfying.
kidNote: The cracking of the brûlée topping is a huge hit with children — let them do the honours with the spoon.
ingredients: 1 vanilla pod, split and seeds scraped
80g caster sugar, plus 4 tbsp for the brûlée topping
steps: Preheat the oven to 150°C/130°C fan. Place four 150ml ramekins in a deep roasting tin.
Heat the cream with the vanilla pod, seeds, and orange zest in a saucepan over low heat until just below boiling. Remove from heat and leave to infuse for 10 minutes, then remove the vanilla pod.
Whisk the egg yolks with the 80g caster sugar until pale and combined. Slowly pour the warm cream over the yolk mixture, whisking gently — don't create bubbles.

Strain through a fine sieve into a jug, then pour into the ramekins. Pour enough boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Bake for 35-40 minutes until just set with a slight wobble in the centre.

Remove from the water bath, cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours. When ready to serve, sprinkle 1 tbsp caster sugar evenly over each custard and caramelise with a blowtorch until deep amber. Leave for 60 seconds to set hard before serving.
tip: Skim any bubbles from the surface of the custard before baking — bubbles bake into small craters on the surface, making it harder to apply an even, glass-smooth caramel crust.

name: BBQ Spatchcock Chicken with Smoky Paprika Rub
description: A whole chicken opened flat and rubbed with a fierce, smoky paprika and garlic paste, then cooked over hot coals until the skin blisters and crisps while the breast stays astonishingly juicy — spatchcocking is the single best technique for cooking a whole chicken on the barbecue. The flat form means even heat distribution and a dramatically reduced cooking time, with a deep, charred flavour from the direct flame that no oven can replicate.
kidNote: Chicken thigh and leg meat is more forgiving and stays juicier — steer children towards these cuts, and check the internal temperature reaches 75°C at the thickest part before serving.
steps: Spatchcock the chicken: place breast-side down on a board. Using strong kitchen scissors, cut along both sides of the backbone from tail to neck and remove it. Flip the chicken over and press firmly on the breastbone with the heel of your hand until it cracks flat.

Mix the olive oil, both paprikas, garlic, cumin, oregano, lemon zest, salt, and pepper to a rough paste. Rub all over the chicken, including under the skin of the breast. Marinate for at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.

Prepare the barbecue for indirect and direct cooking: pile coals to one side. Start the chicken skin-side down over direct heat for 5-6 minutes until the skin colours, then move to the indirect side, close the lid, and cook for 40-45 minutes.
Move back over direct heat for the final 5 minutes to crisp the skin. The chicken is done when the juices run clear and a meat thermometer reads 75°C at the thickest part of the thigh.
Rest the chicken under a loose tent of foil for 10 minutes, then squeeze the lemon halves over and carve. Serve with chargrilled flatbreads and a big green salad.
tip: The overnight marinade is transformative — the acids and spices penetrate the meat far more deeply with time, and the sugars in the paprika caramelise more spectacularly over the coals.

name: Sticky BBQ Pork Ribs with Bourbon Glaze
description: Racks of pork ribs, first slow-roasted in the oven until the meat is falling tender and clinging to the bone, then finished on the barbecue with a bourbon-spiked, molasses-dark glaze that lacquers and caramelises over the coals. This is two-stage cooking that gives you the best of both worlds: guaranteed tenderness from the oven and irreplaceable smokiness from the grill. The kind of ribs that require napkins and complete silence.
kidNote: Remove the rack from the bone for children who struggle with ribs — the tender meat pulls cleanly away and can be served with the sticky glaze on the side for dipping.
ingredients: 2 racks baby back pork ribs (about 1.5kg total)
steps: Preheat the oven to 150°C/130°C fan. Remove the papery membrane from the back of each rack by sliding a knife underneath and peeling it away. Mix the smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, sugar, and salt. Rub all over both racks. Wrap tightly in foil and place on a baking tray.
Bake for 2.5-3 hours until the meat has shrunk back from the bone ends and feels very tender. Open the foil carefully — the steam will be fierce.
While the ribs rest, make the glaze: combine all glaze ingredients in a small saucepan, bring to a simmer, and cook for 5 minutes until slightly thickened.
Brush the ribs generously with glaze and cook on a hot barbecue for 8-10 minutes, turning and basting several times, until deeply caramelised and charred at the edges.
Rest for 5 minutes before cutting into individual ribs.
tip: Removing the membrane (silver skin) from the back of the rack before cooking is non-negotiable — it remains tough and rubbery no matter how long you cook it, acting as a barrier to tenderness.

name: Jerk Chicken Thighs with Mango Salsa
description: Bone-in chicken thighs marinated in a fiercely aromatic jerk paste of scotch bonnet, allspice, and thyme, char-grilled until the skin is blistered and deeply spiced, with a cool, sweet mango salsa to soften the heat — this is the taste of a Jamaican beach on an English summer evening. The jerk marinade builds in layers: heat from the chilli, warmth from the allspice, brightness from the lime.
kidNote: Jerk seasoning can be very hot — reduce the scotch bonnet to a quarter or use a mild red chilli instead, and increase the honey slightly for a sweeter, gentler version for children.
steps: Blitz all jerk paste ingredients (chillies, spring onions, garlic, ginger, soy sauce, olive oil, rum, sugar, spices, lime juice) together in a food processor until smooth. Score the chicken thighs deeply 2-3 times to the bone, then coat thoroughly in the paste. Marinate for at least 2 hours, or ideally overnight.
Make the mango salsa: combine the diced mango, red onion, chilli, lime juice, and coriander. Season with a little salt and refrigerate until needed.
Set up the barbecue for medium heat. Cook the chicken thighs skin-side down for 8-10 minutes until the skin is charred and crisp, watching for flare-ups.
Flip and cook for a further 12-15 minutes until the juices run clear and the internal temperature reaches 75°C at the thickest point. If the skin colours too quickly, move to the indirect heat side.
Rest for 5 minutes and serve with the mango salsa, rice and peas, and lime wedges alongside.
tip: Overnight marinating gives jerk its characteristic depth — the allspice and scotch bonnet need time to penetrate the thick thigh meat. A 2-hour marinade is the absolute minimum.

name: BBQ Pulled Pork Burgers with Pickled Slaw
description: Slow-cooked pork shoulder, smoked over coals until it yields entirely to two forks and falls into glossy, heavily seasoned shreds, piled sky-high into a toasted brioche bun with sharp pickled coleslaw and a final flood of BBQ sauce — this is the American South in a bun. The long, low cooking produces meat of extraordinary tenderness that absorbs smoke and spice in equal measure.
kidNote: Children love pulled pork in a soft bun — ensure the meat is not too spicy and offer the pickled slaw on the side so they can add as much or as little as they like.
steps: Mix the smoked paprika, garlic powder, sugar, cayenne, and salt. Rub generously all over the pork, pressing into every crevice. Leave at room temperature for 1 hour or refrigerate overnight.
Make the pickled slaw: toss the shredded cabbage with cider vinegar, sugar, and salt. Leave for 30 minutes, then drain and mix in the mayonnaise. Refrigerate until needed.

Set up the barbecue for indirect cooking at around 130-140°C. Cook the pork shoulder fat-side up over indirect heat for 4-5 hours until the bark is dark and the internal temperature reads 93°C. Alternatively, after the initial smoking on the BBQ for 1-2 hours, wrap tightly in foil and finish in an oven at 150°C for 3-4 hours.
Rest the pork wrapped in foil for 30 minutes, then shred with two forks. Toss with BBQ sauce.
Toast the brioche buns on the BBQ, pile with pulled pork and top with pickled slaw. Serve immediately.
tip: Pulling pork at 93°C (rather than 85°C when it's technically safe) gives meat of luxurious moistness — those extra degrees break down the last of the collagen into gelatin.

name: Grilled Sea Bass with Salsa Verde & Lemon
